problem: Section 2 defines n as the number of words, but the figure axis and the Quiz Q1 answer call n the number of 'words or cells'. For a memory with a word width greater than one bit these are different numbers, and a student may multiply by the bit count.
fix: Keep one definition: n is the number of addressable words (locations); each march operation reads or writes one whole word. Say 'n is the number of words (addressable locations)' in Q1 and label the figure axis 'words n'.

problem: 'A test must write the aggressor, then read the victim, in both orders' is ambiguous. It can be read as also doing read-victim-then-write-aggressor, which would never excite the fault.
fix: Say: 'A test must write the aggressor and then read the victim, with the aggressor at a lower address than the victim and again with the aggressor at a higher address (both address orders).'

problem: w0, r0 and r1 are defined but w1 is never defined, yet w1 is used in the worked example and in the BIST data-generator bullet, so a student meeting it first in the example has to guess.
fix: Add 'w1 writes 1' next to the definition of w0.

problem: 'March tests cost 10n accesses' overgeneralises: MATS+ costs 5n, as the chapter's own table says. Only March C− in this plot costs 10n.
fix: Caption: 'March C− costs 10n accesses; GALPAT costs about 4n², so it is used only on tiny arrays.'

problem: The sentence lumps transition faults with the need for 'both directions'. A transition fault is excited by writing the opposite value and then the required value (0 then 1, or 1 then 0), which a single ordered pass already does; only some coupling and address-decoder cases need the ascending and descending passes.
fix: Split it: 'Without ordered write-then-read sequences, coupling faults are never excited; without ascending and descending passes, address decoder faults and one of the two coupling address orders are missed.'

problem: 'a BIST pass can fuse in spare rows or columns' confuses BIST with repair. BIST only detects and reports; the repair step is built-in self-repair (BISR), which programmes the spare rows/columns.
fix: Say: 'a BIST pass feeds a built-in self-repair (BISR) block that brings in spare rows or columns.'
